awd_titl_txt: Conference: UIDP Joint Funded PhD Program Workshop
awd_abstract_narration:
This award to the University Industry Demonstration Program (UIDP) is supported by the Directorate of STEM Education (EDU) and the Directorate for Technology, Innovations and Partnerships (TIP) of the U.S. National Science Foundation. Through this project, UIDP will convene a series of events to evaluate the merits and features of a pilot program to establish jointly-funded Ph.D. fellowships.  Building a world-class research and development (R&D) workforce is one of the nation’s most pressing challenges. According to the 2023 NSF Survey of Earned Doctorates, only 34% of recent doctoral graduates in science and engineering fields are employed in academia, down from 54% in 2003. In contrast, the proportion of doctorate recipients with job commitments in industry or business in the United States has more than doubled since 2003, and now comprises nearly half of all employment commitments for doctorate recipients in 2023. While jointly-funded programs exist abroad, there is no long-term U.S.-based program, and few U.S. institutions offer Ph.D. students an opportunity to explore a career in industry through significant experiential learning in a company setting. 

A series of one-day listening sessions followed by a two-day workshop will engage academic, corporate, government, and nonprofit stakeholders to analyze gaps and barriers to partnership, identify nontraditional, high-impact partnership approaches, and consider the creation of a U.S.-based pilot doctoral fellowship program where students are funded jointly by the federal (or state) government and industry. A range of topics will be addressed including: student selection, program life cycle, matchmaking, funding, and compliance.   Meetings will focus on various topical areas including: materials, nanoscience and nanoengineering, biomedical, life sciences, agricultural, engineering, and data science. The goal is to develop the framework for a nationwide program and gain stakeholder engagement in a pilot program that will enhance U.S. capacity and competitiveness in STEM workforce development through model forms of university-industry-government collaboration.

This award is cofunded by the NSF Research Traineeship program and NSF's Directorate for Technology, Partnerships and Innovation. This project aligns with the NSF TIP Directorate as it seeks to support all individuals and increase their interest in, and their access to, career pathways in emerging technology fields. The NSF Research Traineeship (NRT) Program is designed to encourage the development and implementation of bold, new, potentially transformative models for STEM graduate education training.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

Project Outcomes Report - UIDP Joint Funded PhD Program Workshop

UIDP, with support from NSF, convened a series of on-site listening sessions and virtual town halls in 2025, culminating in the NSF-supported workshop, “Expanding STEM PhD Funding Streams,” held September 29-30, 2025, in Alexandria, Virginia. The workshop brought together 145 participants representing 40 companies, 43 universities, and nine additional organizations to advance the development of a jointly funded PhD model that increases funding sources and more directly aligns doctoral training with the needs of the U.S. research and innovation ecosystem.

The workshop charge was to develop one or more workable structures through which multiple parties, including academia, industry, government at all levels, and nonprofits (including philanthropic organizations), could co-invest in STEM PhD education and expand current funding streams. During the working sessions, discussions centered on three core areas:

  1. 1.       Program life cycle. Participants examined the structural elements needed to integrate academic and industry research within a jointly funded PhD model, from program entry through completion. Discussions addressed considerations for program timing within the degree life cycle, student eligibility and selection, the duration and structure of industry engagement, mentorship and oversight, professional development, and cohort building. Participants emphasized the importance of sustained industry engagement and joint university-industry mentorship, while maintaining sufficient flexibility to accommodate differences across disciplines, institutions, and partnership models. The group also identified opportunities to strengthen program identity and support future scaling through cohort-based activities, credentials, and consortium or regional approaches.
  2. 2.       Financial and administrative management. Participants assessed the financial and administrative structures needed to support a jointly funded PhD model across organizations with different fiscal, operational, and compliance requirements. Discussions addressed considerations for partner selection, establishing expectations and agreements, project initiation, student employment classification, funding commitments and administration, indirect costs and financial transparency, and program evaluation. Participants emphasized the value of establishing clear expectations and responsibilities at the outset to reduce administrative barriers and support effective implementation. The group also highlighted the need to balance contributions across funding partners, demonstrate value to participating organizations, and measure outcomes to inform continuous improvement and future scaling.
  3. 3.       Intellectual property (IP) and confidentiality issues. Participants examined how IP and confidentiality could be managed within a jointly funded PhD model involving research conducted across university and industry settings. Discussions addressed considerations for project selection and background IP, approaches to IP rights, invention disclosure, publications and presentations, and protection of confidential information and trade secrets. Participants identified opportunities to reduce IP-related negotiation time and complexity through careful project selection and greater predictability around IP expectations, while maintaining flexibility for different projects and partnership needs. The group also emphasized the need to protect proprietary information while ensuring students can publish, present, and complete their dissertations.

Full results from the workshop and related background research will be available in the forthcoming UIDP workshop report. Following the national workshop, UIDP continued working with participants to translate the findings into a potential pilot model. Discussions included a follow-on virtual town hall for participants, follow-up calls with volunteers, and a pilot framework review meeting with a small group of university and industry representatives on November 20, 2025, in Washington, DC.

Across the initiative, including listening sessions at UC San Diego and the University of Minnesota, seven virtual town halls, the national workshop, and subsequent stakeholder discussions, UIDP engaged 401 unique participants representing 95 universities, 57 companies, and 20 other organizations, including government, nonprofits, philanthropic organizations, societies, and research institutes. Together, these activities demonstrated substantial cross-sector interest in expanding doctoral funding and industry-engaged training, built new connections among stakeholders across the research ecosystem, and mobilized cross-sector stakeholders around the development of a new approach to jointly funded doctoral education.

Findings from the workshop and subsequent stakeholder discussions informed the development of the UIDP Industry-Integrated PhD (I-PhD) Scholars Program, a U.S. pilot designed to strengthen STEM doctoral education by integrating sustained industry research experience into dissertation-based PhD training. The model incorporates many of the priorities identified through the Expanding STEM PhD Funding Streams initiative, including shared investment by university-industry partnerships and an external co-funder, joint academic and industry mentorship, at least one year of dissertation-integrated research at an industry site, and cohort-based professional development. With co-funding support from NSF Directorate for Technology, Innovation and Partnerships (TIP), UIDP launched the pilot in August 2026, translating the workshop findings into an operational model that will support up to 250 doctoral students across its first two cohorts.
